claim: Motor memories of object dynamics are organized categorically in terms of families based on covariation in visual and mechanical properties.
source: We find strong support for the novel hypothesis that motor memories of object dynamics are organized categorically, in terms of families, based on covariation in their visual and mechanical properties.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing that participants encode objects with covarying size and weight as families.

claim: Outlier objects with weights that deviate from the family-predicted weight will never be learned despite causing repeated lifting errors.
source: A striking prediction of this hypothesis, supported by our findings and not predicted by standard associative map models, is that outlier objects with weights that deviate from the family-predicted weight will never be learned despite causing repeated lifting errors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Linear+ condition showing persistent failure to learn outlier weights.

claim: Weight prediction allows production of vertical forces required to raise an object smoothly when lifting from a surface.
source: For example, when lifting an object from a surface, weight prediction allows us to produce the vertical forces required to raise the object smoothly.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on motor control and object manipulation.

claim: When lifting an object for the first time, people estimate its weight based on visual information about its size and material properties.
source: When lifting an object for the first time, people will estimate its weight based on visual information about its size and material properties (Gordon et al., 1993; Flanagan and Beltzner, 2000; Baugh et al., 2012; Baugh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Once an object has been lifted, a memory is formed of its actual weight that can be used to guide subsequent lifts.
source: However, once an object has been lifted, a memory is formed of its actual (i.e. directly sensed) weight, and this memory can be used to guide subsequent lifts of the object (Baugh et al., 2012; Baugh et al., 2016; Johansson and Westling, 1988; Flanagan et al., 2001; Flanagan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on motor memory formation.

claim: Skilled manipulation requires the capacity to form and quickly access representations of object weights in memory.
source: Thus, in addition to intact sensory and motor function, skilled manipulation—and thus the ability to perform most daily tasks—requires the capacity to form, and quickly access, representations of object weights in memory.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the role of weight prediction in motor control.

claim: Participants in the Linear+ group very quickly learned the weights of the training objects.
source: Participants in the Linear+ group very quickly learned the weights of the training objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: At the end of the training phase in the Linear+ group, anticipatory force was strongly correlated with object weight (r = 0.76, 95% CI = [0.66, 0.83]).
source: At the end of the training phase (final eight cycles), anticipatory force was strongly correlated with object weight (r = 0.76, 95% CI = [0.66, 0.83]).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Participants initially estimated that the test object would have the same density as the training objects in the Linear+ group.
source: On the first lift of the test object, the average anticipatory force was 9.00 N (95% CI = [7.68, 10.32]). This suggests that participants initially estimated that the test object would have the same density as the training objects and, therefore, that its weight would be close to the middle of the training object weights (8.83 N).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the measured anticipatory force data.

claim: Participants in the Linear+ group experienced an error of approximately 300 g (~3 N) on the first lift of the test object.
source: Consequently, they experienced an error of approximately 300 g (~3 N), which is close to the weight of a full can of soda and represents fully a third of the anticipated weight.
evidence: This claim is calculated from experimental data on anticipatory force and actual object weight.

claim: Despite large errors, participants in the Linear+ group never learned the test object weight over 40 cycles in the test phase.
source: Remarkably, despite this large error, participants never learned the test object weight over the 40 cycles in the test phase (40 lifts of the test object interspersed with 40 lifts of each training object).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no increase in anticipatory force for the test object.

claim: In the Linear+ group, the anticipatory force for the test object at the end of the test phase was not significantly greater than the family-predicted weight.
source: We found that the anticipatory force was not significantly greater than the family-predicted weight (t(13) = 0.17, p = 0.43).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: At the end of the training phase in the Linear++ group, anticipatory force was strongly correlated with object weight (r = 0.85, 95% CI = [0.72, 0.92]).
source: As expected, at the end of the training phase, anticipatory force was strongly correlated with object weight (r = 0.85, 95% CI = [0.72, 0.92]).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Linear++ group, participants increased their anticipatory force for the test object over 5-10 cycles, reaching an asymptote just below the actual object weight.
source: However, in contrast to the Linear+ group, over the following 5–10 cycles, participants increased their anticipatory force for the test object, reaching an asymptote just below the actual object weight (14.72 N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: In the Linear++ group, the anticipatory force for the test object at the end of the test phase was significantly greater than the family-predicted weight.
source: At the end of the test phase (Figure 2d), the anticipatory force for the test object (13.15 N, 95% CI = [11.56, 14.74]) was significantly greater (t(8) = 3.34, p = 0.0051) than the family-predicted weight (9.65 N, 95% CI = [8.62, 10.68]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There is a limit to how deviant an outlier object can be before it is kicked out of a family and learned as a unique individual.
source: The results of the Linear++ group demonstrate that there is a limit to how deviant an outlier object can be, with respect to a known family, before it is 'kicked out' of that family and learned as a unique individual.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the contrasting results of Linear+ and Linear++ groups.

claim: When error signals from a particular object are sufficiently large, they promote the formation of a separate memory.
source: That is, when the error signals received from a particular object are sufficiently large, they promote the formation of a separate memory.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental results showing learning of extreme outliers.

claim: The failure to learn the test object in the Linear+ group is not due to an inability to visually distinguish the test object from neighboring training objects.
source: Note that the adaptation to the test object in the Linear++ group demonstrates that participants could visually distinguish the test object from the neighboring training objects. Thus, we can conclude that the striking failure to learn the test object in the Linear+ group is not due to an inability to visually identify the test object amongst the similar-looking training objects.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Linear++ group's ability to learn the extreme outlier.

claim: In the Uncorr+ group, there was poor differentiation of object weights in the earliest trial cycles.
source: In the earliest trial cycles, there was poor differentiation of the object weights, showing that uncorrelated mappings are more difficult to learn than linear mappings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e and comparison with Linear groups.

claim: By the end of the training phase, the Uncorr+ group achieved accuracy comparable to the Linear groups, with anticipatory force strongly correlated with object weight (r = 0.72, 95% CI = [0.62, 0.80]).
source: Nevertheless, by the end of the training phase the Uncorr+ group achieved accuracy comparable to the Linear groups, with anticipatory force being strongly correlated with object weight (r = 0.72, 95% CI = [0.62, 0.80]).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Participants in the Uncorr+ group succeeded in adapting their anticipatory force for the test object during the test phase.
source: However, as can be seen in Figure 2e, during the test phase participants in the Uncorr+ group succeeded in adapting their anticipatory force for the test object.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: In the Uncorr+ group, the anticipatory force for the test object at the end of the test phase was significantly greater than the average force for the training objects.
source: At the end of the test phase (Figure 2f), participants' anticipatory force for the test object (10.48 N, 95% CI = [9.50, 11.46]) was significantly greater (t(11) = 4.06, p = 0.00094) than the average force for the training objects (8.68 N, 95% CI = [8.44, 8.92]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The failure to learn the test object in the Linear+ group is due to the structured object family, rather than lack of a sufficient error signal.
source: The learning of the test object observed in the Uncorr+ group confirms that the failure to learn the test object in the Linear+ group is due to the structured object family, rather than the lack of a sufficient error signal.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing Linear+ and Uncorr+ group results.

claim: In the Linear+ group, there was significant generalization from the test object to training objects at both the start and end of the test phase.
source: For the Linear+ group (Figure 2g), we found significant generalization both at the start (t(13) = 5.47, p = 1.1e−4) and the end of the test phase (t(13) = 5.56, p = 9.2e−5), with no significant change (t(13) = 1.68, p = 0.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Linear++ group, generalization from the test object to training objects was significant at the start of the test phase but greatly reduced at the end.
source: For the Linear++ group (Figure 2h), there was significant generalization at the start of the test phase (t(8) = 5.61, p = 5.1e−4) that was greatly reduced at the end of the test phase, with a significant change over time (t(8) = 3.95, p = 0.0042).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Linear++ group, participants initially encoded the extreme outlier as a family member, but then formed a separate memory of this object.
source: This shows that participants initially encoded the extreme outlier as a family member, but then formed a separate memory of this object.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the generalization data showing change over time.

claim: In the Uncorr+ group, there was no evidence of generalization from the test object to training objects at the start or end of the test phase.
source: For the Uncorr+ group (Figure 2i), we found no evidence of generalization at the start (t(11) = 1.90, p = 0.085) or the end of the test phase (t(11) = 0.45, p = 0.66), and no change over time (t(11) = 1.90, p = 0.084), consistent with encoding each object individually (Figure 2i).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Response times decreased during the training phase for both linear and uncorrelated size-weight mappings.
source: As shown in Figure 2j, response times decreased during the training phase for both the linear and the uncorrelated size-weight mappings, but there was a consistent temporal cost associated with movement preparation when size and weight were uncorrelated as compared to linearly related.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA on log-transformed response times revealed significant main effects of Group and Epoch, but no interaction.
source: A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA on log-transformed response times revealed significant main effects of Group (F(1, 33) = 5.79, p = 0.022) and Epoch (F(3, 99) = 13.039, p = 0.30e−7), but no interaction (F(3, 99) = 0.80, p = 0.49).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Encoding each object individually resulted in a temporal cost compared to encoding objects as a family, even at the end of the test phase.
source: These results show that, even at the end of the test phase, encoding each object individually resulted in a temporal cost compared to encoding the objects as a family.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the response time data analysis.

claim: There was no evidence of increased response times on switch trials in the Linear++ condition.
source: However, we found no evidence of increased response times on these 'switch trials'.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of response time data in the Linear++ condition.

claim: In the Linear++ condition, the average response time when lifting the outlier after a family member was only 3 ms longer than the predicted value.
source: In the Linear++ condition, the average response time when lifting the outlier after a family member group was only 3 ms longer (95% CI = [−156, 159]) than the predicted value, and the average response time when lifting a family member after the outlier was 25 ms faster (95% CI = [−129, 79]) than the predicted value.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of response time data.

claim: The data provide no evidence for the idea that the large temporal cost observed in the Uncorr+ condition is a switch cost.
source: Thus, our data provide no evidence for the idea that the large temporal cost observed in the Uncorr+ condition is a switch cost.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lack of switch costs in the Linear++ condition.

claim: The data are consistent with the idea that there is a selection cost associated with mapping the visual stimulus onto the appropriate category.
source: However, our data are consistent with the idea that there is a 'selection cost' associated with mapping the visual stimulus onto the appropriate category.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the response time patterns observed.

claim: Both +Linear and ++Linear groups quickly and accurately learned the weight of the test object when it was presented individually during the training phase.
source: As expected, both groups quickly and accurately learned the weight of the test object when it was presented individually during the training phase (Figure 3a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and c.

claim: At the start of the test phase in the +Linear and ++Linear groups, participants began to treat the outlier and the four family objects as a single family.
source: However, at the start of the test phase (beginning at trial cycle 31), it is evident that participants in both groups began to treat the outlier and the four family objects as a single family.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in anticipatory forces.

claim: Brief exposure to an object family can reorganize the memory of a previously learned individual object, such that it is assimilated into the family.
source: These results show that even brief exposure to an object family can reorganize the memory of a previously learned individual object, such that it is assimilated into the family.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the +Linear and ++Linear group results.

claim: In the +Linear group, the anticipatory force for the outlier at the end of the test phase was not significantly greater than the family-predicted weight.
source: At the end of the test phase (Figure 3b), the anticipatory force for the outlier in the +Linear group (10.01 N, 95% CI = [9.18, 10.84]) was not significantly greater (t(10) = 1.23, p = 0.12) than the family-predicted weight (9.49 N, 95% CI = [9.11, 9.86]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Participants in the +Linear group did not re-learn the actual weight of the outlier after it was assimilated into the family.
source: Thus, participants in the +Linear group did not re-learn the actual weight of the outlier after it was assimilated into the family.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the statistical analysis showing no significant learning.

claim: In the ++Linear group, the anticipatory force for the outlier at the end of the test phase was significantly greater than the family-predicted weight.
source: In the ++Linear group, the anticipatory force for the outlier at the end of the test phase (12.76 N, 95% CI = [11.14, 14.39]) was significantly greater (t(10) = 4.19, p = 0.00093) than the family-predicted weight (9.76 N, 95% CI = [9.47, 10.04]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the +Linear group, there was minimal impact on learning in the 1:1 phase where the relative frequency of outlier and family objects was equivalent.
source: As shown in Figure 3a, in the +Linear group there was minimal impact on learning in the 1:1 phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The family effect cannot be accounted for by the greater relative frequency of the family objects.
source: These findings demonstrate that the family effect cannot be accounted for by the greater relative frequency of the family objects.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the 1:1 phase results showing persistent family effect.

claim: Category boundaries that determine whether an object is encoded as a family member or as a separate individual may depend on within-category variability.
source: A fundamental question is whether such boundaries are fixed or flexible. Research on both perceptual and conceptual categorization has shown that category boundaries may depend on within-category variability (Rips, 1989; Huttenlocher et al., 2000; Clayards et al., 2008), and that category labeling can exhibit hysteresis whereby the point at which the perceived category changes depends on the direction of change (Williams et al., 1986; Hock et al., 1993; Poltoratski and Tong, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on categorization.

claim: Both Linear➚ and Linear➘ groups quickly and accurately learned the weights of the training objects.
source: First, both groups quickly and accurately learned the weights of the training objects, with anticipatory forces that were strongly correlated with actual object weights by the end of the training phase (r = 0.81, 95% CI = [0.73, 0.87] in Linear➚; r = 0.84, 95% CI = [0.77, 0.89] in Linear➘).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In both Linear➚ and Linear➘ groups, the anticipatory force generated on the first lift of the test object was close to the middle of the weights of the family objects.
source: Second, in both groups the anticipatory force generated on the first lift of the test object was close to the middle of the weights of the family objects (9.40 N, 95% CI = [8.10 10.70] in Linear➚; 8.07 N, 95% CI = [5.93, 10.22] in Linear➘).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data.

claim: At the end of the initial 20 cycles of the test phase in the Linear➚ group, learning of the 1.2 kg test object was not significant.
source: Third, at the end of the initial 20 cycles of the test phase, during which the test object weight remained at its initial value, learning of the 1.2 kg test object was not significant (Linear➚: t(8) = −0.58, p = 0.71), whereas learning of the 1.5 kg test object was significant (Linear➘: t(8) = 2.15, p = 0.032).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: At the end of the initial 20 cycles of the test phase in the Linear➘ group, learning of the 1.5 kg test object was significant.
source: Third, at the end of the initial 20 cycles of the test phase, during which the test object weight remained at its initial value, learning of the 1.2 kg test object was not significant (Linear➚: t(8) = −0.58, p = 0.71), whereas learning of the 1.5 kg test object was significant (Linear➘: t(8) = 2.15, p = 0.032).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Linear➚ group, the anticipatory force at the end of the test phase was not significantly greater than the family-predicted weight, despite the test object weighing 1.5 kg.
source: However, the anticipatory force at the end of the test phase (11.02 N, 95% CI = [9.44, 12.60]) was not significantly greater (t(8) = 1.81, p = 0.054) than the family-predicted weight (9.72 N, 95% CI = [9.43 10.01]), and was still substantially less than the actual weight (14.72 N; Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Despite the test object weighing 1.5 kg at the end of the test phase in the Linear➚ group, it was not kicked out of the family, in contrast to the equally heavy test object in the Linear++ group.
source: Thus, despite the fact that the test object weighed 1.5 kg at the end of the test phase, it was not 'kicked out' of the family, in contrast to the equally heavy test object experienced by the Linear++ group in our first experiment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing Linear➚ and Linear++ results.

claim: There was a significant difference in the anticipatory force for the outlier object at the end of the test phase between the Linear➚ and Linear++ groups.
source: A direct comparison between the Linear➚ and Linear++ groups showed a significant difference in the anticipatory force for the outlier object at the end of the test phase (t(16) = 2.20, p = 0.043).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing the two groups.

claim: In the Linear➘ group, the anticipatory force at the end of the test phase was significantly greater than the family-predicted weight and indistinguishable from the actual weight.
source: At the end of the test phase, the anticipatory force (11.69 N, 95% CI = [10.35, 13.03]) was significantly greater (t(8) = 4.35, p = 0.0012) than the family-predicted weight (9.20 N, 95% CI = [8.65, 9.75]) and indistinguishable from the actual weight (11.77 N; Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Once a separate memory was formed for the test object in the Linear➘ group, it continued to be encoded as an individual even when its weight deviation decreased to the level that the Linear+ group failed to learn.
source: Thus, once a separate memory was formed for the test object, it continued to be encoded as an individual even when its weight deviation decreased to the level ( + 300 g, or 33%) that the Linear+ group failed to learn.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Linear➘ group results.

claim: There was a significant difference in the anticipatory force for the outlier object at the end of the test phase between the Linear➘ and Linear+ groups.
source: A direct comparison between the Linear➘ and Linear+ groups showed a significant difference in the anticipatory force for the outlier object at the end of the test phase (t(21) = −3.68, p = 0.0014).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing the two groups.

claim: According to the object families hypothesis, an outlier object is encoded categorically as either a family member or an individual.
source: According to the object families hypothesis, an outlier object is encoded categorically as either a family member or an individual.
evidence: This is a statement of the theoretical hypothesis being tested.

claim: A given participant should either fully learn the weight of an outlier object or not learn at all, depending on their particular threshold for kicking out an object from a family.
source: As a consequence, a given participant should either fully learn the weight of an outlier object or not learn at all, depending on their particular threshold for 'kicking out' an object from a family.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the object families hypothesis.

claim: The object families hypothesis predicts a bimodal distribution of estimated weights across participants for certain outliers.
source: Assuming that the threshold weight at which an outlier is kicked out of a family varies across participants, the object families hypothesis predicts that for certain outliers, there will be a bimodal distribution of estimated weights across participants (separating learners from non-learners).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the object families hypothesis.

claim: The associative map hypothesis predicts that partial learning will be observed and that there will be a unimodal distribution in the amount of learning, regardless of the weight of the outlier.
source: In contrast, the associative map hypothesis predicts that partial learning will be observed and that, assuming learning rates across participants are normally distributed, there will be a unimodal distribution in the amount of learning, regardless of the weight of the outlier.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the associative map hypothesis.

claim: The web-based task was designed to closely mirror the laboratory task.
source: The web-based task was designed to closely mirror the laboratory task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The results for the Linear+ and Linear++ groups in the web-based experiment were very similar to those observed for the corresponding groups in the first experiment.
source: The results for the Linear+ and Linear++ groups in the web-based experiment (Figure 5b and e) were very similar to those observed for the corresponding groups in our first experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data across experiments.

claim: Similar learning processes were engaged in the web-based experiment despite the use of visual dynamics without haptic feedback.
source: This indicates that similar learning processes were engaged despite the use of visual dynamics without haptic feedback (Danion et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the similarity of results and supported by citation.

claim: On average, the Linear+ group in the web-based experiment did not learn the outlier, whereas the Linear++ group exhibited substantial, but not complete, learning.
source: On average, the Linear+ group did not learn the outlier, whereas the Linear++ group exhibited substantial, but not complete, learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the web-based experiment.

claim: For the Linear+ group in the web-based experiment, the single-Gaussian model was favored over the two-Gaussian mixture model.
source: As expected, for the Linear+ group, in which learning of the weight of the outlier was not observed, the single-Gaussian model was favored (ΔAIC = −4.6; relative likelihood = 10.0).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical model comparison of experimental data.

claim: For the Linear++ group in the web-based experiment, the distribution was clearly bimodal and better captured by the two-Gaussian model.
source: In contrast, for the Linear++ group, the distribution was clearly bimodal, separating participants who either did or did not learn the outlier weight. This bimodal distribution was better captured by the two-Gaussian model (ΔAIC = 7.0, relative likelihood = 33.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical model comparison of experimental data.

claim: In the Linear++ web-based group, the greater of the two Gaussian means representing learners lies almost perfectly on the actual outlier weight.
source: In the Linear++ group, the greater of these two means (8.48 N, 95% CI = [7.98, 8.89])—representing the learners—lies almost perfectly on the actual outlier weight (dashed line, 8.83 N), whereas the lesser of the two means (5.43 N, 95% CI = [4.91, 6.08])—representing the non-learners—is very close to the family-predicted weight (4.91 N, 95% CI = [4.79, 5.03]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the mixture model fits.

claim: In the Linear+ web-based group, while most participants did not learn the outlier weight at all, there was a small subgroup who fully learned this weight.
source: Thus, while most participants in the Linear+ group did not learn the outlier weight at all, there was a small subgroup who fully learned this weight.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the two-Gaussian mixture model fit.

claim: For the Linear- group in the web-based experiment, the distribution of anticipatory forces for the outlier object were best fit by the single-Gaussian model.
source: For the Linear- group, the distribution of anticipatory forces for the outlier object at the end of the test phase were best fit by the single-Gaussian model (ΔAIC = −3.7, relative likelihood = 6.4), whereas the two-Gaussian model was preferred for the Linear-- group (ΔAIC = 29.3, relative likelihood = 2.3e + 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical model comparison of experimental data.

claim: For the Linear-- group in the web-based experiment, the two-Gaussian model was preferred over the single-Gaussian model.
source: For the Linear- group, the distribution of anticipatory forces for the outlier object at the end of the test phase were best fit by the single-Gaussian model (ΔAIC = −3.7, relative likelihood = 6.4), whereas the two-Gaussian model was preferred for the Linear-- group (ΔAIC = 29.3, relative likelihood = 2.3e + 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical model comparison of experimental data.

claim: The results of the large-sample web-based experiment clearly support the object families hypothesis over the associative map hypothesis.
source: Overall, the results of this large-sample web-based experiment clearly support the object families hypothesis over the associative map hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the bimodal distribution results.

claim: At the level of single participants, the outlier was either encoded as a family member or identified as a distinct individual.
source: At the level of single participants, the outlier was either encoded as a family member, in which case lift errors were ignored, or it was identified as a distinct individual, in which case lift errors drove complete learning of the outlier's weight.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the bimodal distribution results.

claim: Similar bimodality was observed in the laboratory experiments.
source: Notably, similar bimodality was also observed in the laboratory experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by mixture model analysis of laboratory data.

claim: The two-Gaussian model outperformed the single-Gaussian model for the combined Linear+ and +Linear group in the laboratory experiments.
source: The two-Gaussian model outperformed the single-Gaussian model for the combined Linear+ and +Linear group (ΔAIC = 13.3, relative likelihood = 772.8) and the resulting clustering yielded 20 non-learners and five learners.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical model comparison of laboratory data.

claim: In the combined Linear++ and ++Linear group, the two-Gaussian model outperformed the single-Gaussian model.
source: In the combined Linear++ and ++Linear group, the two-Gaussian model outperformed the single-Gaussian model (ΔAIC = 9.8, relative likelihood = 134.3), with the resulting clustering yielding six non-learners and 14 learners.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical model comparison of laboratory data.

claim: When considering only the non-learners in the combined Linear+ and +Linear group, the anticipatory force for the outlier was very similar to the family-predicted weight.
source: When considering only the non-learners in the combined Linear+ and +Linear group, the anticipatory force produced for the outlier at the end of the test phase (8.98 N, 95% CI = [8.50, 9.47]) was very similar to the family-predicted weight (9.33 N, 95% CI = [8.97, 9.68]), as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the clustered laboratory data.

claim: When considering the small subset of learners in the combined Linear+ and +Linear group, the anticipatory force for the outlier showed that these participants fully learned the actual weight.
source: Strikingly, when considering the small subset of learners in the combined Linear+ and +Linear group, the anticipatory force for the outlier at the end of the test phase was 11.71 N (95% CI = [11.34, 12.08]), showing that these participants fully learned the actual weight of the outlier (11.77 N).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the clustered laboratory data.

claim: The results strengthen the main conclusion that memories of the motor properties of objects are organized categorically.
source: Thus, these results strengthen our main conclusion that memories of the motor properties of objects are organized categorically.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the bimodality results across experiments.

claim: The mechanical properties of objects, which are fundamentally important to human motor control, have received little attention in theories of object memory.
source: However, the mechanical properties of objects, which are fundamentally important to human motor control, have received little attention in theories of object memory.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the literature on object memory theories.

claim: The majority of tasks we perform involve physical objects, and skilled interaction with these objects depends critically on our ability to predict their mechanical properties.
source: The majority of tasks we perform involve physical objects, and skilled interaction with these objects depends critically on our ability to predict their mechanical properties.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about motor control.

claim: For many objects we interact with, dexterous performance requires accurate predictions of weight.
source: For many of the objects that we interact with, dexterous performance requires accurate predictions of weight (Gordon et al., 1991; Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001; Flanagan et al., 2006; Johansson and Flanagan, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The question of how motor memories of the myriad objects we interact with are represented and organized has not been addressed.
source: However, the question of how motor memories of the myriad objects we interact with are represented and organized has not been addressed.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the literature on motor memory.

claim: According to a well-known neuroanatomical framework, the dorsal visual pathway supports visual processing for action, whereas the ventral visual pathway supports visual processing for perception.
source: According to a well-known neuroanatomical framework for understanding visual processing in the primate brain, the dorsal visual pathway, in parietofrontal cortex, supports visual processing for action, whereas the ventral visual pathway, in ventrotemporal cortex, supports visual processing for perception (Goodale and Milner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There is abundant evidence that parietofrontal cortex is engaged in computations for reaching and grasping movements.
source: The control of these actions involves mapping these visual features onto motor commands to move and shape the hand (Salinas and Abbott, 1995; Arbib, 1981; Jeannerod, 1981; Pouget and Snyder, 2000), and there is abundant evidence that parietofrontal cortex is engaged in such computations (Jeannerod et al., 1995; Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001; Castiello and Begliomini, 2008; Grafton, 2010; Battaglia-Mayer and Caminiti, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Some evidence suggests that motor memories linking visual and mechanical properties could involve parietal and premotor regions of the dorsal pathway.
source: Some evidence suggests that such memories could involve parietal and premotor regions of the dorsal pathway (Chouinard et al., 2005; Jenmalm et al., 2006; Chouinard et al., 2009; Freedman and Assad, 2009; van Nuenen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The maintenance of durable memory representations of objects is more commonly associated with the ventral visual pathway.
source: However, the maintenance of durable memory representations of objects is more commonly associated with the ventral visual pathway (Bruce et al., 1981; Ungerleider and Haxby, 1994; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Grill-Spector et al., 2001; Erez et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Category selectivity is a well-established organizational feature of ventrotemporal cortex.
source: Given that category selectivity is a well-established organizational feature of ventrotemporal cortex (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014), it seems plausible that the ventral pathway also plays a role in categorizing the mechanical properties of objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Object weight is represented in the lateral occipital complex (LOC) in the context of lifting.
source: Consistent with this view, it has been shown that, in the context of lifting, object weight is represented in the lateral occipital complex (LOC) (Gallivan et al., 2014), an object-selective ventral region also known to be active during reaching and grasping (Culham et al., 2003; Monaco et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LOC does not appear to represent object mass that can be inferred when simply viewing objects interacting.
source: On the other hand, LOC does not appear to represent object mass that can be inferred when simply viewing objects interacting (Schwettmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Predictive encoding of object weight has been demonstrated in single-cell recordings of Purkinje neurons.
source: For instance, predictive encoding of object weight has also been demonstrated in single-cell recordings of Purkinje neurons (Allan et al., 2015; Mason et al., 2006), which may arise from cerebellar internal models of the dynamics of different types of objects (Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001; Imamizu et al., 2000; Bursztyn et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is considerable evidence for the role of prefrontal cortex and the striatum in perceptual category learning.
source: Likewise, there is considerable evidence from human imaging studies and non-human primate neurophysiological studies for the role of prefrontal cortex and the striatum in perceptual category learning (Freedman et al., 2001; Ashby and Maddox, 2005; Reber et al., 1998; Vogels et al., 2002; Seger and Miller, 2010; Antzoulatos and Miller, 2011; Antzoulatos and Miller, 2014; Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018; Raz and Saxe, 2020), but it remains unknown whether these areas are also recruited in organizing objects based on their learned motor properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Current theories of motor learning often focus on graded generalization of learning across various stimulus and motor parameters.
source: Current theories of motor learning often focus on graded generalization of learning across various stimulus and motor parameters as a revealing feature of the underlying computations (Krakauer et al., 2000; Thoroughman and Shadmehr, 2000; Donchin et al., 2003; Ingram et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Graded patterns of generalization have been taken as evidence that motor learning fundamentally involves associating contextual features with target motor parameters in a continuous multi-dimensional space.
source: In particular, graded patterns of generalization have been taken as evidence that motor learning fundamentally involves associating contextual features of a movement with the target motor parameters in a continuous multi-dimensional space, often termed an associative map.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of motor learning theory.

claim: The theoretical significance of this study is that it provides evidence for a fundamentally different type of organization—motor memories of objects are organized categorically, into families.
source: The theoretical significance of our study is that it provides multiple, converging pieces of evidence for a fundamentally different type of organization—motor memories of objects are organized categorically, into families.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The key result is the family effect itself, wherein an outlier object is persistently encoded as a family member, despite greatly deviating from its expected weight.
source: Our key result is the family effect itself, wherein an outlier object is persistently encoded as a family member, despite greatly deviating from its expected weight.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main experimental finding.

claim: The prediction of an associative map account is that outliers would eventually be learned, since they are visually and haptically discriminable from the family.
source: In contrast, the prediction of an associative map account is that these outliers would eventually be learned, since they are visually and haptically discriminable from the family (as shown by the accurate learning in the Uncorr+ condition).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the associative map model and supported by data from the Uncorr+ condition.

claim: The way that the outlier object was classified had a dramatic effect on outlier-to-family generalization.
source: We found that the way that the outlier object was classified—either as a family member or an individual—had a dramatic effect on outlier-to-family generalization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on generalization patterns.

claim: When the outlier object was classified as a family member, strong generalization was observed, whereas when it was classified as an individual, generalization was substantially reduced.
source: When the outlier object was classified as a family member, strong generalization was observed, whereas when it was classified as an individual, generalization was substantially reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on generalization patterns.

claim: These results strongly support the idea that motor memories of objects are organized categorically, rather than continuously.
source: These results strongly support the idea that motor memories of objects are organized categorically, rather than continuously, which would predict graded generalization as a function of error magnitude and sensory similarity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the generalization results.

claim: By eliciting separate visual classification of the outlier and the family objects, we were able to suddenly shut off inter-object error generalization.
source: By eliciting separate visual classification of the outlier and the family objects, we were able to suddenly 'shut off' inter-object error generalization.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental manipulation and results.

claim: One interpretation of the Linear➚ finding is that first experiencing the 1.2 kg outlier, and then experiencing incrementally increasing weights, broadened the category by increasing the within-category variability.
source: One interpretation of this finding is that first experiencing the 1.2 kg outlier, and then experiencing incrementally increasing weights, broadened the category by increasing the within-category variability, as shown in perceptual and conceptual categorization (Rips, 1989; Huttenlocher et al., 2000; Clayards et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research on categorization.

claim: Another possible account for the Linear➚ finding is that category labels are sticky, and that once the test object was labeled as a family member, there was resistance to relabeling it as an individual.
source: Another possible account for this finding is that category labels are 'sticky', and that once the test object was labeled as a family member, there was resistance to relabeling it as an individual, similar to the hysteretic effects reported in perceptual categorization (Williams et al., 1986; Hock et al., 1993; Poltoratski and Tong, 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research on categorization.

claim: It is possible that learning the extreme 1.5 kg outlier as a distinct individual object caused the category boundary for the training objects to contract.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that learning the extreme 1.5 kg outlier as a distinct individual object caused the category boundary for the training objects to contract, such that a 1.2 kg outlier remained outside the learned family, perhaps because the individuated outlier effectively forms a competing category.
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation of the Linear➘ results.

claim: Work on sensorimotor adaptation has shown that participants do not become aware of visual or force perturbations that are introduced gradually.
source: Note that work on sensorimotor adaptation has shown that participants do not become aware of visual or force perturbations that are introduced gradually (Kagerer et al., 1997; Malfait and Ostry, 2004; Klassen et al., 2005; Saijo and Gomi, 2010; Criscimagna-Hemminger et al., 2010; Roemmich and Bastian, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the experiment with a gradually increasing outlier weight, participants did not adapt and continued to predict the outlier weight based on the family density.
source: In contrast, in our experiment with a gradually increasing outlier weight, participants did not adapt (i.e. they continued to predict the outlier weight based on the family density).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Linear➚ group.

claim: The reason that participants learned the 1.5 kg outlier when introduced abruptly, but not when introduced gradually, may be that they are sensitive to the change in error, as opposed to error per se.
source: The reason that participants learned the 1.5 kg outlier when introduced abruptly, but not when introduced gradually, may be that they are sensitive to the change in error, as opposed to error per se.
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation of the contrasting results.

claim: Recent research on motor learning and adaptation has emphasized the role of explicit processes.
source: Although the formation of motor memories has historically been viewed as a largely implicit process, recent research on motor learning and adaptation has emphasized the role of explicit processes.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of recent motor learning research.

claim: When reaching under a visuomotor rotation, participants often learn to use an explicit re-aiming strategy to reduce movement errors.
source: For example, when reaching under a visuomotor rotation, participants often learn to use an explicit re-aiming strategy to reduce movement errors (Mazzoni and Krakauer, 2006; Anguera et al., 2010; Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011), and can quickly recall and implement this strategy when re-exposed to the rotation at a later time (Taylor et al., 2014; Huberdeau et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: People often have explicit knowledge of the weights of objects they interact with.
source: In the context of object manipulation, it is clear that people often have explicit knowledge of the weights of objects they interact with.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about object manipulation.

claim: When lifting familiar objects, weight estimates can be quite accurate, although research on weight illusions shows that these estimates are biased by expected weight.
source: When lifting familiar objects, these estimates can be quite accurate, although research on weight illusions shows that these estimates are biased by expected weight (Flanagan and Beltzner, 2000; Flanagan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous research has shown that greater working memory resources are required when lifting unusually weighted objects than when lifting normally weighted objects.
source: The use of explicit knowledge is believed to require working memory and previous research has shown that greater working memory resources are required when lifting unusually weighted objects than when lifting normally weighted objects (Baugh et al., 2016; Flanagan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When participants lift objects that are encoded as a family, this categorical encoding is largely implicit, requiring little to no explicit processing.
source: Based on these findings, we speculate that when participants lift objects that are encoded as a family, this categorical encoding is largely implicit, requiring little to no explicit processing.
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation based on prior research findings.

claim: Explicit processing may contribute to encoding an object that is similar in appearance to the family as an outlier.
source: In contrast, we suspect that explicit processing does contribute to encoding an object that is similar in appearance to the family as an outlier.
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation.

claim: Explicit processing may be required when learning the weights of multiple individual objects, as in the Uncorr+ condition.
source: Likewise, explicit processing may be required when learning the weights of multiple individual objects, as in our Uncorr+ condition.
evidence: This claim is speculative interpretation supported by the response time data.

claim: As people become more experienced at classifying objects into separate families, the contribution of explicit knowledge will likely diminish and lifting will become more implicit and automated.
source: In general, as people become more experienced at classifying objects into separate families, the contribution of explicit knowledge will likely diminish and lifting will become more implicit and automated.
evidence: This claim is speculative prediction about learning over time.

claim: Any form of memory engaged in a motor control task can be considered as a motor memory, whether that is an explicit declarative memory or an implicit procedural memory.
source: From our perspective, any form of memory engaged in a motor control task can be considered as a 'motor memory', whether that is an explicit declarative memory or an implicit procedural memory.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the authors' perspective.

claim: The findings open the door for future work that connects theories of human category learning with theories of motor control.
source: By showing that dexterous object manipulation relies on learned representations of categories (and individuals), our findings open the door for future work that connects theories of human category learning, developed in the context of perception and cognition, with theories of motor control.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: Many existing process-level models of category learning posit a mechanism that allows for the creation of a new category in memory when an observation deviates sufficiently from previously learned categories.
source: However, focusing more narrowly on accounting for the present findings, it is notable that many existing process-level (i.e. trial-by-trial) models of category learning posit a mechanism that allows for the creation of a new category in memory when an observation deviates sufficiently from previously learned categories (Ashby and Maddox, 2005; Hartigan, 1975; Carpenter and Grossberg, 1987; Clapper and Bower, 1991; Anderson, 1991; Love et al., 2004; Vanpaemel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on category learning models.

claim: Various treatments of category learning can be viewed as instances of non-parametric Bayesian models that leverage the hierarchical Dirichlet process.
source: These various treatments can all be viewed as instances of non-parametric Bayesian models that leverage the hierarchical Dirichlet process, a statistically principled approach to clustering data into a theoretically infinite number of components (Teh et al., 2005; Griffiths et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on Bayesian models.

claim: A recent motor control model has been developed based on the hierarchical Dirichlet process approach.
source: A recent motor control model has been developed based on this approach (Heald et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: At present, the Heald et al. model cannot account for the current results because there is no mechanism through which the visual properties of the objects can be linked together to form a family.
source: However, at present this model cannot account for our results because there is no mechanism through which the visual properties of the objects—which are encoded as discrete cues—can be linked together to form a family.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the limitations of the cited model.

claim: Learning a family of objects based on covarying size and weight is presumably just one example of a more general tendency to compactly encode the covariability of observable sensory features and latent mechanical properties.
source: In general, learning a family of objects based on covarying size and weight, as in this study, is presumably just one example of a more general tendency to compactly encode the covariability of observable sensory features and latent mechanical properties.
evidence: This claim is speculative generalization from the findings.

claim: Previous work has shown that people can learn more complex structures in motor control tasks, but has not distinguished between categorical and associative representations.
source: Previous work has shown that people can learn more complex 'structures' in motor control tasks (e.g. visuomotor rotations and skews), but has not distinguished between categorical and associative representations (Braun et al., 2009; Braun et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Categorical encoding allows for more robust interpolation and extrapolation from past sensorimotor experience by shoehorning ambiguous new items into predictable categories.
source: First, it allows for more robust interpolation and extrapolation from past sensorimotor experience by shoehorning ambiguous new items into predictable categories.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the benefits of categorical encoding.

claim: Categorical encoding reduces the temporal costs associated with specifically identifying objects.
source: Second, it reduces the temporal costs associated with specifically identifying objects, which would involve deeper traversal into object memory.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the benefits of categorical encoding, supported by the response time data.

claim: When working with multiple objects from the same family, categorical encoding conserves working memory resources that would otherwise be expended on object individuation.
source: Third, when working with multiple objects from the same family, this strategy conserves working memory resources that would otherwise be expended on object individuation.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the benefits of categorical encoding.

claim: Categorical organization conserves long-term memory resources by maintaining only abstract descriptions of relevant family structure, rather than a detailed map of all sensorimotor properties.
source: Lastly, categorical organization also conserves long-term memory resources by maintaining only abstract descriptions of relevant family structure, rather than a detailed map of all sensorimotor properties, helping to address the curse of dimensionality.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the benefits of categorical encoding.

claim: Learning about individual objects may increase accuracy in some circumstances, but this would come at the cost of significantly increased demands on attention, cognitive control, and memory.
source: In contrast, although learning about individual objects may increase accuracy in some circumstances, this would come at the cost of significantly increased demands on attention (for visual recognition), cognitive control (for switching between memories), and memory (for storage).
evidence: This claim is speculative about the costs of individual object encoding.

claim: In combination with context-sensitive reflexes and other rapid corrective mechanisms, a categorical memory of object properties affords tradeoffs between accuracy and memory that can be balanced as needed to support skillful manipulation of many different kinds of objects.
source: Therefore, in combination with context-sensitive reflexes and other rapid corrective mechanisms, a categorical memory of object properties affords tradeoffs between accuracy and memory that can be balanced as needed to support our unmatched ability to skillfully manipulate many different kinds of objects.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the functional role of categorical memory in motor control.
